lines: The foreman counts every breath we take, and docks us for the ones we waste.
Twelve hours at the bellows and my arms still ache in my sleep.
Soot in my bread, soot in my bed, soot in my prayers.
Mind where you step, the floors here have been known to burn through boots.
Last week a vat boiled over green and the whole shift wept for a day.
I came here for the wages. I stay because I cannot remember the way home.
They say the masters upstairs never sweat. Must be nice, up there.
Keep your sleeves away from anything that glows, hums, or smiles at you.
The heat takes your eyebrows first, then your patience, then your hearing.
My father worked these same benches, and his hands looked like mine by thirty.
Another cart of ore came in at dawn, and another comes tomorrow. There is always another cart.
The overseer says hurry, the master says careful. Nobody ever says rest.
Something in the crucible screamed this morning. We were told not to ask.
You have the look of someone who fights. Fighting must be easier than this.
A good shift is one where everybody walks out on the legs they walked in on.
We sing at the benches to keep the rhythm. Join in, if you know the words.
The smoke here never lifts. I have not seen a clear star in three winters.
Careful with the brass fittings, they bite when they are still warm.
Rumour says the great work is nearly finished. Rumour said that last year too.
My lungs rattle like a sack of nails, but the coin still feeds my little ones.
One of the apprentices turned blue yesterday, not cold, just blue. He still is.
Ale tastes better when you have earned it beside the furnace.
Do not touch the pipes marked in red. Do not even look at them long.
The masters want it faster, finer and cheaper. Pick two, I tell them, quietly.
Half the hands here have burns. The other half have not been here long.
I dream of cool rivers and clean shirts, nothing grander than that.
They pay on the last day of the week, and the taverns know it too.
Whatever they are building, it is hungry. It eats iron by the ton.
A spark landed in my hair at noon. I smelled it before I felt it.
If you see the foreman, I am fetching water. Very slowly, very far away.
The night shift swears the machines whisper. The day shift swears louder to drown them out.
Every tool here is older than me, and most of them are better tempered.
I lost two fingers to the press. The foreman docked me a day for the mess.
Rest your feet a moment if you like. Mine have forgotten how.
Three weeks at sea and the ground still rolls under me like a swell.
Shore leave is short and the taverns are many. I mean to see them all.
The fog here swallows ships whole. We came in by bell and prayer.
Saw a tentacle wider than our mainmast off the northern shoals. Nobody believes me.
The captain owes us a month of wages and a barrel of excuses.
A storm took our foresail and half the galley. We ate wet biscuit for nine days.
Never whistle aboard ship, lass. You will call up a wind you cannot pay for.
I have seen water so black and still you could walk on the stars in it.
Got my first tattoo in a port like this one. Cannot remember which.
The sea gives you salt in your wounds and silver in your pocket, rarely both.
Our cook drowned in a flat calm. Leaned over for a look and something leaned back.
Looking to sign on? We are always short a hand after a long voyage.
If you hear singing from the water at night, stop your ears and pray.
A sailor ashore is like a fish in a tree. Help me find the tavern again.
My wife is the sea, my mistress is the rum, and both of them want me drowned.
The fog bell has rung all day. Somewhere out there a ship is lost.
We hauled a net of bones up off the reefs. Not fish bones, either.
Spent my whole pay in two nights. Worth every copper, I think, though I cannot recall it.
Mind the gulls, they steal anything shiny. One took a ring right off my finger.
The old salts say a drowned city lies under the bay, bells and all.
Smell that? The wind is turning, and there will be rain by dusk and a gale by midnight.
A good knot holds a ship together. A bad one buries a crew.
I have sailed past ice that groaned like a giant in pain.
The press gangs are about tonight. Keep your head down and your boots quick.
Our ship rides low with cargo. I do not ask what is in the crates.
My legs miss the deck already. Land is too still, and it makes me uneasy.
Pirates chased us two days running. We lost them in this very fog.
You fight on land, I fight the sea. Mine never tires of the battle.
The bosun keeps a lucky fish bone. Gods help us the day he loses it.
Every scar on these hands has a story, and every story ends with rope.
Spotted lights under the waves last voyage, moving against the current.
A dry bed and a hot meal. That is all a sailor dreams of at sea.
When the moon rises red, no captain worth his salt will leave the harbour.
Fair winds to you, stranger, wherever your road ends.
Crates up, crates down, crates in, crates out. That is my whole life.
The harbour master wants this hold empty by dusk, and my back disagrees.
Watch your purse near the warehouses. The fog hides more than ships.
Lost a crate of spices last night. The harbour master thinks I ate it.
Coil that rope for me, would you? If not, then step aside, please.
A hawser snapped this morning and nearly took a man's head clean off.
Somebody keeps cutting the mooring lines at night. Three boats drifted out last week.
The fog rolls in so thick I cannot see my own hands on the rope.
Heavy cargo today, iron, they say. It felt more like lead and sorrow.
The harbour master counts every barrel twice and pays every man once, and late.
Thieves on the piers again. Saw a shadow slipping between the bales.
Mind the gaps in the planks. The water underneath is colder than a grave.
I unloaded a cage last week. Whatever was inside it kept knocking politely.
My shoulders carry this whole harbour. Ask anyone, or better, ask my shoulders.
Ships come from everywhere, but the cargo always smells of tar and fish.
The tide waits for nobody, and neither does the harbour master.
There is a crate in the end warehouse nobody will touch. It hums at night.
Rope burns heal, but the splinters stay with you for life.
Some days the fog is so close you can hear whispers from the next pier.
Paid by the load, I am. So no chatter, unless you are lifting.
Rats the size of dogs down in the holds. Bring a cudgel if you go aboard.
The ships from Vel Morrath carry incense and silence. Strange cargo, both.
A sailor tried to sell me a map to sunken treasure. Third one this month.
Busy morning. Four ships in, two out, and one missing in the fog.
Strong arms, good knots, short memory. That is what a dockhand needs.
The harbour master hangs smugglers off the end of the long pier. As a warning.
Cargo from the forges comes in black and greasy. Ruins every shirt I own.
Grab the other end of this plank? My mate went for ale an hour ago.
If a crate leaks something blue, do not touch it, and do not tell anyone.
The cranes creak like old men, and so do I by the end of the day.
Fog bell, gull cry, a captain shouting. That is the music of the docks.
Somebody stole a whole anchor off the pier last night. How do you even carry one?
Lend me your eyes a moment. Is that a ship out there, or just more fog?
Mind your step on the wet stones. The harbour has drowned better walkers than you.
The nets came up heavy today. Mostly cod, one boot, and something with too many eyes.
Cold sea, cold hands, cold supper. Still better than starving.
Fish do not bite in the fog. They just lie still and listen.
My grandmother mended nets on this same pier. I still tie her knots.
Pulled up an eel as long as my boat. Cut the line and rowed home fast.
The herring are late this year. When the herring are late, something is wrong.
Something keeps tearing my nets from below. Clean cuts, like a blade.
The sea was kind this morning. That usually means it is planning something.
Fresh mackerel, caught at dawn. Smell them, still all salt and silver.
Lost my brother to a squall three summers back. I still set his place at supper.
If you ever net a white fish with a face, throw it back. Trust me.
The water out past the point is so cold it burns like fire.
I mend nets in the evenings. My fingers know the work better than my head.
Caught a crab once that spoke. Only one word, but it was my name.
A good catch feeds the family a week. A bad one teaches patience.
The gulls follow my boat home every day like an army of beggars.
Old fishers say never row out on the dark of the moon. I listen to old fishers.
Strange lights under the bay last night. The fish fled before them.
My hands are cracked from the salt. A little grease, and they bend again.
The deep fish come up when the storms come. Ugly things, and worth a fortune.
You smell of the road, and I smell of the sea. Neither is pleasant.
Out before dawn, back before dusk, if the fog allows it.
Found a silver ring inside a cod yesterday. Gave it to the temple, just in case.
The sea feeds us and the sea takes us. That is the bargain.
My boat is old, but she floats, and that is all I ask of her.
The water runs warm near the old wreck. The fish will not go near it.
Sold my catch for half its worth. Merchants smell want like sharks smell blood.
A seal followed me home and sat on my doorstep crying all night.
Keep away from the black rocks at low tide. Things wait in the pools.
When the nets come up empty three days running, we pray, and then we row farther.
I salt the fish for winter. The whole house smells of it until spring.
Pulled a drowned bell from the bottom once. It rang on its own that night.
Calm water, full nets, dry boots. Some days the gods are generous.
The cold sea keeps its secrets well, but now and then it coughs one into my net.
